verdict.reasoning: Patient reports difficulty breathing after being stung by a bee/wasp a few minutes prior: 'I'm kind of struggling to breathe at the moment. I got stung by a wasp recently... It was just a few minutes ago.' and 'one of the two? Yeah, it was one of the two.'

He describes and shows a rash with redness and a puncture on the arm: 'I've got a bit of a rash on my arm where I got stung' and 'It's slightly red, yeah. And kind of there's a bit of a. Like a hole where... the puncture mark.'

Patient reports sensation of swelling, while clinician does not see swelling: 'potentially there's a bit of swelling in my lips and tongue. Feels a bit weird.' and clinician notes 'your, your lips don't seem swollen to me right now.'
He explicitly mentions anxiety and worry about worsening: 'I'm feeling like slightly anxious' and 'I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse. I just wanted to speak to someone.'

He denies acute severe shortness of breath: 'Do you feel that you've got difficulty breathing right now...?' 'I don't feel like it's like particularly acute...' and clinician says, 'Your breathing seems all right to me right now.'
No history of anaphylaxis and no EpiPen: 'Have you got a history of anaphylaxis?' 'Not that I know of, no.' and 'Have you ever been given an EpiPen?' 'I haven't, no.'

He reports occasional anxiety and no medication: 'Can I ask, do you suffer from anxiety or panic attacks...?' 'Yeah, sometimes. Occasionally.' and 'Have you ever been on medication for that?' 'No. No.'
'Do you have any history of any kind of illnesses at all?' 'I've had eczema before. That's kind of the major thing.'
Specifically not on anxiety medication: 'Have you ever been on medication for that?' 'No. No.'
'Have you got a history of any allergies to anything?' 'I'm allergic to penicillin.'

No food or pet allergies: 'do you have allergies to any kind of cats or dogs or pets...?' 'Not that I know of. Yeah, I've been around dogs and cats.' and 'And you've got no food allergies as far as you're aware?' 'No.'
He reports no relevant family history: 'in your family, is any history of any illnesses or any history of any kind of acute.' 'Not that I think is particularly relevant, no, I don't have any.'
Social history: 'Are you working at the moment?' 'Yes.' 'What do you work as?' 'I am a computer scientist.' 'And you're living alone?' 'Yes.' 'Do you have any pets at home?' 'I have a cat.'
Exam notes rash, mild redness, puncture mark: 'That looks okay to me. Right now. Does it look red to you at the moment?' 'It's slightly red...' and 'Yeah. The puncture mark. Yeah.'

Clinician sees no visible lip/oral swelling: 'your, your lips don't seem swollen to me right now' and after oral exam: 'based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing... I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction,' with no mention of visible oral swelling; this supports absence of visible swelling.

Normal respiratory effort/talking: 'Your breathing seems all right to me right now' and 'based on how you look, how you're talking to me and how you're breathing... I don't feel that you're having a life threatening allergic reaction.'
Clinician explicitly notes absence of stridor: 'you might have something called stridor... Thankfully you don't have anything like that right now.'

No local swelling beyond mild rash: 'Now, is there any swelling around that area that you can see? I couldn't see any.' Patient: 'Not particularly... just a bit... blotchy and a bit of a rash. It doesn't feel like particularly swollen.'
Assessment of localized allergic reaction to insect sting: 'it seems to me that this is a localized allergic reaction.' and 'one of the two? Yeah, it was one of the two [bee or wasp].'
Patient is anxious about progression: 'I'm feeling like slightly anxious' and 'I'm just kind of a bit anxious that it might get a bit worse.'

Antihistamine recommendation: 'you can buy the counter, you can get pyritone or chlorphenamine and you can take one tablet, four milligrams, up to about six times a day. Okay? Or you can just take a one a day.'

Education on anaphylaxis signs and urgent care: 'I'm just going to warn you about what those signs and symptoms are... swelling of the lips, difficulty breathing, you might have something called stridor...' and 'if anything changes, if anything deteriorates, either make an appointment with us or go straight to ae... in some cases... it's better to go straight to AE.'

Advice to watch for spreading erythema/warmth and consider antibiotics: 'If the redness in your arm spreads and it feels hot or, you know, you have signs of any localised infection, we may need to think about other treatments like an antibiotic.'
Plan to provide written information: 'I'm going to leave some information about anaphylactic reactions just for you to read about it.'

Reassurance and advice to reconsult: 'Sometimes a chat is all you need to calm things down.' and 'Get back to us if you're feeling worried. Just have a low threshold for having a chat with us.' and 'Come back to us if you have any further issues.'
